A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SASFT research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Substantial changes to experimental settings can be distinguished from retained content.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-switching evaluations, multilingual benchmark results, and ablations across five models, including additional experiments and significance tests in its appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports revised original evaluations and additional benchmark results, SAE-configuration analyses, and controlled code-switching induction experiments in Appendices I–K.

M1.justification: SASFT retains the same language-feature identification procedure, thresholded pre-activation auxiliary loss, and combined training objective. SASFTEnhance moves from Appendix C to Appendix F without changing its definition. SFT+Penalty is an added comparator, not a modification of SASFT.

E1.justification: V1 trains on proprietary instruction data; v2 replaces it with a mixture of public sources, including KULLM, Tulu3, WildChat, BelleGroup, Multialpaca, Flores, and GSM8KInstruct (Appendix C). This substantially replaces the training corpus, beyond changing sample counts. The three principal target languages and existing evaluation prompt families remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds SFT+Penalty to the principal comparisons and threshold ablation in Tables 1–3. Its variant experiment also adds SASFTReduce alongside SASFTEnhance in Table 9, enabling a direct comparison absent from v1 Table 4. These additions materially strengthen the comparison set.

E3.justification: Training sets change from 230k/130k to nominal 210k/110k samples. Appendix E replaces shared learning-rate and loss-weight settings with model-specific choices and changes GRPO batch size from 32 to 256. Table 2 switches from Chinese 230k to Chinese 110k training. V2 also adds MGSM accuracy scoring and protocols for the new SAE-configuration and induction experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds feature-consistency tests across SAE widths and sparsities at layers 19–25 (Appendix J), plus controlled feature enhancement on 100 originally non-code-switching samples (Appendix K). Existing layer, feature, threshold, and enhancement analyses receive revised evidence, including a direct reduction-versus-enhancement comparison.

E5.justification: V1's Appendix E and Table 5 report one-tailed two-proportion Z-tests; v2 removes this significance analysis without equivalent tests or confidence intervals. V2 newly discloses eight evaluations per prompt in Table 6. This establishes repeated evaluation reporting, not an increase in training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced under revised settings. For example, Table 1's large-data Gemma-2-2B Chinese SFT/SASFT ratios change from 1.02/0.32% at 230k to 0.74/0.42% at 210k. These are not same-setting performance changes. V2 additionally reports MGSM accuracy, capability results for further training settings, and new robustness and induction findings.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a mathematical definition of the SFT+Penalty objective in Eq. (10). The existing task, SAE, SASFT, and enhancement-loss definitions remain substantively unchanged; the enhancement loss is merely renumbered. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows complete code-switching elimination from four cases in v1 to one in v2. The central contributions—SAE-based mechanistic analysis, SASFT, and reducing unwanted switching while preserving multilingual capabilities—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix K strengthens the interpretation to bidirectional causal evidence for language-feature control, while Appendix J newly argues that feature identification and SASFT are robust to SAE configuration choices. Conversely, Section 3.3.1 softens v1's Chinese-token interpretation into a predictive association with upcoming switching. The original limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V1 states that its private training data cannot be released and code release is planned. V2 supplies a public-data construction recipe, source/language counts, and a code/data availability statement. Appendices D–E substantially expand evaluation composition, software-stack, model-specific hyperparameter, optimization, and training-time information. External availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Wang et al. and Nie et al. on internal mechanisms of language mixing, and expands SAE references with Shi et al. and Fang et al. V2 also adds detection, data, and software references and removes the statistical-testing reference. The central research positioning remains largely intact.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative is largely retained. Changes include the SASFT title prefix, localized rewrites, a separate language-feature background subsection, author/header and citation-style updates, and appendix reorganization. The submission checklist is removed and an LLM usage statement added; most substantive expansion consists of new experimental content.

P2.justification: V2 expands main tables with comparator rows and an MGSM column, adds detailed data/settings and capability tables, and introduces SAE-similarity heatmaps and an induction plot. It removes the significance table, redraws Figures 6–7, and adopts a different conference layout with substantially changed display placement.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a major reproducibility weakness through a documented public-data training recipe and reported code/data access. The token-penalty baseline, direct reduction-versus-enhancement comparison, and new robustness and induction studies substantially strengthen evaluation and mechanistic support. Removing significance tests and retaining overly broad superiority claims despite GRPO wins in Table 1 weaken reporting, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.
